meaning: Zero Budget Natural Farming (ZBNF) — farming method popularized by Subhash Palekar that avoids purchased chemical/external inputs, relying instead on soil microorganisms activated via cow dung/urine-based preparations.
"Mother Earth, Goddess of Nourishment" — the foundational metaphor that soil already contains everything a plant needs and nurtures all life without discrimination.
Soil microorganisms; the biological agents that convert locked/unavailable soil nutrients into plant-available form.
A fermented liquid culture (cow dung + cow urine + other ingredients) used to multiply beneficial soil microorganisms; applied to soil, not to leaves.
A cow dung/urine-based seed treatment applied before sowing to protect and activate seeds.
Mulching — covering soil to retain moisture and return organic matter; ZBNF recognizes multiple types (straw mulch, soil mulch, live/crop mulch).
Balance of air and moisture in the soil (soil aeration + moisture management), as opposed to waterlogging.
Traditional practice of alternating monocot (cereal) and dicot (legume) crop rows in intercropping/rotation.
Monocot crops (e.g., ragi/finger millet, jowar/sorghum, paddy) — single-leaf/grain family.
Dicot crops (e.g., groundnut, cowpea, horse gram) — legume/pulse family.
Fine capillary root hairs, the actual site of water/nutrient absorption in plants — typically located at the canopy drip-line, not the trunk base.
Weeds. In ZBNF philosophy, weeds are generally cut and left in place rather than removed from the field.
Self-development — a seed's ability to grow into a full plant unaided, from seed to seed.
Self-nourishing — the forest's ability to feed itself without external input.
"Light farming" — designing crop placement and layering by each plant's sunlight requirement.
"Water farming" — using atmospheric moisture and groundwater recharge rather than only extraction.
"Nutrient farming" — the practice of unlocking existing soil nutrients via microbes rather than adding external fertilizer.
A nitrogen-fixing bacterium that lives in root nodules of leguminous (dicot) plants and converts atmospheric nitrogen into plant-usable nitrate.
Root nodules — small swellings on legume roots that house Rhizobium colonies; not to be confused with root-knot nematode disease.
The protein formed when raw sugar (from photosynthesis) combines with nitrogen; its accumulation is the plant's actual physical growth.
"Bund soil" — soil taken from field edges/commons never exposed to chemicals, used as a microbial starter in Jeevamrutha.
Tall crops (e.g. jowar, maize) planted amid a field so birds perch on them and prey on pest insects — a natural pest control method.
Solid/dry form of Jeevamrutha (dung + jaggery + pulse flour + bund soil, dried and powdered) for use on rain-fed fields without irrigation.
Stunted, immature pods that result when the same legume crop is grown repeatedly in the same spot, causing root-nodule growth to stall.
The clumping together of soil particles into a more granular structure, improving water infiltration in heavy black (regur) soils.
Traditional practice of treading nitrogen-rich green leaves (honge, neem, tangadi, ekke) into a paddy field before transplanting.
Gravity — the force that draws monsoon clouds across long distances and pulls fallen rain down into the soil.
Capillary action — the process by which water (and dissolved nutrients) already in the soil rises back up toward the surface as it warms and evaporates.
The leaf canopy of a plant, described as its "face" — where stress, hunger, and excess water all visibly show up first.
The process by which a plant releases the majority of absorbed water as vapor through its leaves to maintain internal balance.
The dormant, leaf-shedding period after harvest (autumn) during which a plant's remaining roots decompose, loosening the soil for the next season.
Native/landrace seeds — traditional, non-hybrid seed varieties that grow larger plants with deeper roots, making them more drought-resilient.
Taproot — the deep primary root that draws moisture and nutrients from deep soil during drought stress, when surface moisture is unavailable.
Mulching — the third of ZBNF's four wheels, comprising three sub-types: soil mulching (tillage/weeding), live mulching (companion cropping), and dry mulching (straw cover).
Pre-monsoon deep tillage done to draw nutrients from decomposed crop residue into the soil ahead of the first rains.
The multi-tier/multi-storey planting system (big tree → small tree → shrub → bush → vine/grass) used mainly in horticulture and orchards.
"Trap crop" — a deliberately planted sacrificial crop (e.g. castor, arali) that draws pest insects away from the main crop; must not be sprayed.
The practice of gently treading and breaking the central shoot of a young ragi/aarka plant to stimulate tillering (more side shoots) about 20 days later.
"Jeevana dravya" — organic matter formed from carbon and nitrogen combining in soil; its accumulation improves soil's physical, chemical, and biological properties.
Organic carbon — a key soil fertility index; ideal is 2.5-3%, most farmland today sits near 0.2%, ZBNF plots can reach 3.5-4%.
Carbon-to-Nitrogen ratio (~10:1) required for organic carbon to permanently bind with nitrogen and form humus, rather than escaping back as CO2.
A soft-wooded, nitrogen-fixing tree planted among orchard rows to supply nitrogen to young horticultural saplings.
A fast-growing, soft-stemmed nitrogen-fixing tree used similarly to Glyricidia in orchard intercropping design.
A widely-held misconception that plants suffer from roots physically "stepping on" each other; the real cause is competition for scarce nutrients, especially nitrogen.
Staggered-timing planting — planting fast, tall "giant trees" first and adding companion trees around them only after they've gained height, to avoid shade competition.
Marigold — the only known natural remedy for root-knot nematode disease; its roots secrete Alpha-Terthienyl, which kills the pathogen; also attracts pollinators and can be sold.
The nematode-killing chemical compound secreted by marigold roots.
A vigorous, sprawling legume used as ground cover between young orchard trees to suppress weeds and fix nitrogen while awaiting the main crop's maturity.

A seed's built-in dormancy/protection mechanism that prevents every fallen seed from sprouting (natural population control); Beejamrutha treatment safely helps seeds overcome this, raising germination from 60-80% to over 95%.
The step in Beejamrutha preparation where a cloth bundle of dung is suspended in water overnight to release its microorganisms.
"Predator microorganisms" that emerge once a Jeevamrutha drum's microbial population outgrows its space, beginning to destroy the excess — the reason liquid Jeevamrutha must be used within 7-10 days.

The five classical elements (earth, water, fire, air, space) whose approximate proportions in plant/animal bodies are used to explain why only ~1.5% of a plant's mass ("earth element") comes from soil.
ZBNF's fourth and final wheel — the balanced state of soil pores holding roughly equal air and water, achieved via Jeevamrutha microbes and intercrop root decomposition.
A neem-leaf-based botanical spray for sap-sucking pests (aphids, mealybugs); made with neem leaf, cow urine, and fresh dung, steeped 24-48 hours; must be used within 1-2 days.
A multi-leaf botanical spray (neem plus several other leaves) for fruit and pod borers; steeped 48 hours in cow urine; can be stored up to 6 months.
A stronger tobacco-and-hot-chili-based preparation for stem borers, boiled and applied by spot-spraying or syringe injection directly into the borer's hole.
A simple sap-sucking pest remedy made from benzoin resin (sambrani) steeped in cow urine for 7-8 days.
A fermented sour-buttermilk fungicide made from native cow's milk, curdled, churned, diluted, and soured for 2 days; safe enough to drink; stores up to 6 months.
Drainage channels dug between trees in waterlogged or clay-heavy land to prevent fungal disease caused by standing water.
Natural pest suppression that emerges when many intercrop species attract a mix of parasitic and predator insects, which then keep pest populations in check without any spraying.
A potent botanical concoction made from ten kinds of leaves plus dung and cow urine, fermented 15-30 days; used against stubborn pests that don't respond to Neemastra/Brahmastra/Agniastra.
Fungal-driven sap oozing from wounds or nicks in tree trunks/stems, common in coconut; triggered by physical injury combined with excess moisture or heat.
A banana disease causing leaves to dry from the tip and yellow/brown before dropping, rooted in an "it needs lots of water" mindset that leads to overwatering.
A thorny, leaf-folding plant used in a botanical spray against thrips/mite damage; also treated as a beneficial weed to be cut only after flowering but before seeding.
The post-monsoon (rabi) and monsoon (kharif) growing seasons; sowing a crop in the wrong season strips it of the natural disease resistance it would otherwise have.
The leaf process converting CO2 + water + sunlight into raw sugar (C6H12O6), releasing oxygen and surplus water back to the atmosphere.
The pigment that makes leaves green and drives photosynthesis.
The process by which a plant releases part of its manufactured food around its roots to feed soil microbes, which in turn convert unavailable soil nutrients into a plant-usable form.
Traditional irrigation practice of building a raised basin around a tree trunk and pooling water there; becomes ineffective once the canopy outgrows the basin.
The full spread of a plant's leaf canopy; the root system generally spreads to roughly the same width, which is where water and nutrients should be applied.
The sun's apparent northward movement (Dec 21-Jun 20) and southward movement (Jun 21-Dec 20); used to decide the correct north-south row orientation for crops.
A basic crop-planning classification: large horticultural "giant trees" (mango, cashew, tamarind) versus sun-hungry grain crops (rice, ragi, wheat, jowar).
A five-layer crop-planning framework: giant tree, small tree, shrub, small plant/vine, and tuber-plus-litter — combined for maximum yield per plot.
A unit of light intensity (light from a candle at one foot); giant trees and grain crops need over 7,000 foot-candles of peak summer sun to fruit well.
A sugarcane seed-saving technique: each bud/eye is cut with an uneven ratio (1/3 base, 2/3 tip) and Beejamrutha-treated individually, cutting seed use from ~4,000 kg/acre to 250-400 kg/acre.
Within the sugarcane furrow system, the row reserved specifically for household food grains (rice, ragi, wheat) rather than cash-crop vegetables.
The second flush of cane that regrows from the stubble/roots after the first harvest, without replanting.
The leftover cane leaves and trash after harvest, spread as mulch on the neighbouring row rather than burned.
A perennial nitrogen-fixing tree used in banana orchards alongside moringa and glyricidia to keep supplying nitrogen after legume intercrops get shaded out.
The dappled sunlight created as breeze moves the leaves of tall nitrogen-fixing trees, letting filtered light and partial shade reach the crops below.

The full recipe for a key fungicide: milk is cultured into curd, churned to buttermilk without butter forming, then fermented 2-3 days until sharply sour before diluting for spray; used against Panama Wilt, mildew, and other fungal issues.
A viral banana disease where leaves suddenly shrink into broom-like clusters; the guest advises against the common practice of burning infected plants, favoring mulch and extra Jeevamrutha instead.
The very low-moisture state a ripe coconut must be dried down to (only 2-3 spoons of water left inside) before it's suitable for sowing as seed.
A nursery bed used for sprouting seeds, nuts, or paddy seedlings before transplanting.
Plain dried, powdered, sieved native-cow dung stored on its own (without the fermented Jeevamrutha additions), used as a simpler soil input.

A beneficial fungus present in solid Jeevamrutha; white grubs and dung beetles that feed on the Jeevamrutha ingest it and are killed from within, giving natural grub control without a separate pesticide.

A block of several rows (e.g. 3-4) set aside within a tall grain crop like jowar for a shorter companion crop (safflower, linseed, chana), making the shorter crop easier to manage than if scattered through every row.
A grid-pattern single-seedling wide spacing (8, 10, 12, or 16 inches square) for direct-sown or transplanted rice, allowing each plant's roots to spread freely on all sides.
The conventional practice of transplanting 4-5 rice seedlings together per spot out of fear of poor germination; blocks airflow and sunlight, causing fungal blast disease and lower yield.
Leaving cut grain stalks lying in the row for a few days after harvest so remaining nutrients in the still-green leaf/stem transfer into the grain, reducing chaff/empty grains.
Direct dry-cultivation of rice without a flooded nursery: seed is soaked 6 hours, treated in Beejamrutha, and sown 1-2 seeds per spot in a checkerboard grid with solid Jeevamrutha.
Companion plants grown together in a polyculture whose roots interlock underground and exchange nutrients, while also disrupting pest life cycles compared to monocropping.

The dark organic substance formed when 10 carbon particles bond with 1 nitrogen particle as dead organisms and plant waste decompose; 1kg of it absorbs about 6L of atmospheric moisture per day, explaining why some natural-farming fields look dry on top yet stay green.
Acclimatizing shade-raised nursery seedlings to open sunlight for 2-3 days before transplanting, to prevent transplant shock and wilting.
A traditional row-spacing pattern for direct-sown ragi/millet where an extra 1-foot row is inserted between the main 2x2ft grid lines to increase plant density without crowding.
A fungicide made by fermenting butter-skimmed buttermilk (diluted 1:4 with water) for 2-5 days until sharply sour, used against yellowing, blast, and leaf-curl diseases.

The strongest-tier botanical pesticide, made from ten kinds of leaves (neem, papaya, custard apple, etc.) plus tobacco, chili, garlic, turmeric and ginger, fermented in shade for 40 days; used when Agniastra/Brahmastra fail to control severe pest outbreaks.
